title: What is the difference between a DOMAIN event (internal to one bounded context, triggers side effects across aggregates, often via an in-process event bus like Spring Application Events) and an INTEGRATION event (published to Kafka for cross-service communication), and why must integration events act as an Anti-Corruption Layer — exposing only a stable, versioned schema (Avro/Protobuf + Schema Registry) and keyed by the aggregate-root ID for per-aggregate ordering — rather than leaking the producer's internal model?

s1_definition.profdef: A domain event is an internal event raised and handled within a single bounded context, usually in-process through a mechanism like Spring Application Events, to trigger side effects across aggregates inside that one service; it may freely reference the service's internal domain model because it never leaves the service. An integration event is a published, cross-service event carried over a broker like Kafka to let other services react; it must act as an Anti-Corruption Layer, exposing only a deliberately designed, stable, versioned schema — typically Avro or Protobuf governed by a Schema Registry — and keyed by the aggregate-root ID so a broker partition preserves per-aggregate ordering, rather than leaking the producer's internal model to consumers.
s1_definition.analogy: Inside National Bank of India's transfer department, when a transfer completes, a note is passed between desks in the same room — "transfer done, update the daily tally, recompute the fee" — written in the department's own shorthand because only people in that room read it. That shorthand note is a domain event. But when the department wants to tell the SMS department and the statement department in other buildings, it does not hand them its private shorthand; it fills out an official, standardized form with only the fields outsiders are allowed to see, versioned so old forms still work. That official form is an integration event, and the rule that you never show outsiders your private shorthand is the Anti-Corruption Layer.
s1_definition.oneliner: Domain events are private, in-process, and may use your internal model; integration events are public, broker-carried, versioned contracts that shield consumers from your internals and are keyed by aggregate ID for ordering.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A domain event is an internal event raised and handled within a single bounded context, usually in-process through a mechanism like Spring Application Events, to trigger side effects across aggregates inside that one service; it may freely reference the service's internal domain model because it never leaves the service. An integration event is a published, cross-service event carried over a broker like Kafka to let other services react; it must act as an Anti-Corruption Layer, exposing only a deliberately designed, stable, versioned schema — typically Avro or Protobuf governed by a Schema Registry — and keyed by the aggregate-root ID so a broker partition preserves per-aggregate ordering, rather than leaking the producer's internal model to consumers.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Inside National Bank of India's transfer department, when a transfer completes, a note is passed between desks in the same room — "transfer done, update the daily tally, recompute the fee" — written in the department's own shorthand because only people in that room read it. That shorthand note is a domain event. But when the department wants to tell the SMS department and the statement department in other buildings, it does not hand them its private shorthand; it fills out an official, standardized form with only the fields outsiders are allowed to see, versioned so old forms still work. That official form is an integration event, and the rule that you never show outsiders your private shorthand is the Anti-Corruption Layer.

**One line to remember:** Domain events are private, in-process, and may use your internal model; integration events are public, broker-carried, versioned contracts that shield consumers from your internals and are keyed by aggregate ID for ordering.

sections.s2_technical:
A domain event lives entirely inside one bounded context — one microservice. It represents something meaningful that happened in the domain, like TransferCompleted, and it exists to decouple side effects within that service. When the transfer aggregate completes, instead of directly calling the fee recalculation and the daily-tally update, it publishes a domain event and lets in-process listeners react. In Spring you do this with ApplicationEventPublisher and @EventListener, and crucially with @TransactionalEventListener so listeners fire after the transaction commits. Because the event never leaves the process, it can carry rich references to the internal domain model — entities, value objects, internal enums — without any coupling cost, since there is no external consumer to protect. Domain events keep a single service's internals clean and decoupled across its own aggregates.

An integration event is a fundamentally different thing even if it describes the same business fact. It is published to a broker like Kafka specifically so other services, owned by other teams, can react. The moment an event crosses the service boundary, its schema becomes a contract, exactly like a public API, and every consumer couples to it. This is why an integration event must act as an Anti-Corruption Layer, a Domain-Driven Design idea meaning you deliberately translate from your internal model to an external representation at the boundary so your internals cannot corrupt, or be corrupted by, the outside world. In practice this means the integration event exposes only a curated set of fields that consumers legitimately need, named and shaped for external stability, never your internal entity serialized directly. If you publish your internal model, then every refactor of your internals becomes a breaking change for every consumer, and you have recreated the tight coupling microservices were meant to eliminate.

Three concrete practices make integration events safe. First, a stable, versioned schema using a binary, schema-first format like Avro or Protobuf, governed by a Schema Registry that enforces compatibility rules so you can add fields without breaking old consumers and can evolve safely. Second, keying by the aggregate-root ID — for example the account ID — so that all events for the same aggregate land on the same Kafka partition and are therefore consumed in order, which matters because out-of-order events about one account could corrupt derived state. Third, an explicit translation step in the producer that maps the internal domain event or aggregate to the external integration-event schema, which is the Anti-Corruption Layer made real in code.

A senior engineer ties the two together with a common pattern: a domain event fires in-process when something happens, a handler translates it into an integration event written to the transactional outbox in the same transaction, and the relay publishes the integration event to Kafka. This cleanly separates concerns — domain events for internal decoupling, integration events for reliable, versioned, ordered cross-service communication — and it keeps the internal model free to evolve behind the stable external contract. The anti-pattern to avoid is treating them as the same thing and publishing raw internal domain events to Kafka, which leaks your model and couples everyone.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India's transfer service completes a transfer and must both react internally and tell other services. Conflating internal and external events would couple everyone to its internal model.

Problem 1 — When a transfer completes, the transfer service internally needs to recompute the account's daily transfer total and update an internal fee cache. These are side effects across aggregates within the one service. This is exactly a domain event handled in-process, carrying the rich internal model freely.

Problem 2 — The notification and statement services, owned by other teams, also need to know. If the transfer service simply serializes its internal TransferAggregate to Kafka, then renaming an internal field later breaks both downstream services. This is why the external message must be an integration event acting as an Anti-Corruption Layer with only curated, versioned fields.

Problem 3 — Multiple transfers on the same account must be processed in order by consumers, or a statement balance could be computed from stale ordering. This is why the integration event is keyed by the account (aggregate-root) ID so Kafka preserves per-account order.

What the code will do: a runnable demo shows the transfer service raising an internal `TransferCompletedDomainEvent` carrying the internal model, handled in-process by `DailyTotalListener` and `FeeCacheListener`. A `IntegrationEventTranslator` (the Anti-Corruption Layer) maps that internal event into a slim, versioned `TransferCompletedIntegrationEvent` with only external fields, keyed by account ID, which is then published to a simulated Kafka. A `NotificationConsumer` in another service consumes only the integration event and never sees the internal model.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer of Rs.50000 on account SAV2001 to beneficiary BENEF-77 completing on the transfer service.

Step 1: The internal `TransferAggregate` completes and raises a `TransferCompletedDomainEvent` that carries the whole internal model, including internal-only details like a ledger reference and a risk bucket. This event is in-process and never leaves the service.

Step 2: The in-process bus delivers the domain event to internal listeners. `DailyTotalListener` adds the amount to the account's daily total and freely reads the internal ledger reference; `FeeCacheListener` refreshes a cache using the internal risk bucket. Using internal details here is completely fine because there is no external consumer to protect.

Step 3: The `IntegrationEventTranslator`, which is the Anti-Corruption Layer, also receives the domain event. It translates the internal model into a slim `TransferCompletedIntegrationEvent` containing only the curated external fields — event ID, account ID, beneficiary, amount, timestamp — and deliberately drops the internal ledger reference and risk bucket.

Step 4: The translator publishes the integration event to Kafka keyed by the account ID (the aggregate-root ID), so all events for SAV2001 land on the same partition and are consumed in order. The schema is versioned, so consumers are shielded from future internal changes.

Step 5: The `NotificationConsumer` in a different service consumes only the integration event and sends an SMS. It never sees the producer's internal model, so the transfer team can refactor its internals freely without breaking the notification team.

Final output:

```
14:30:00 INFO    [DOMAIN] DailyTotalListener: added Rs.50000 to daily total for SAV2001 (ledgerRef=LEDGER-....)
14:30:00 INFO    [DOMAIN] FeeCacheListener: refreshed fee cache for risk bucket 2
14:30:00 INFO    [ACL] translated domain event → integration event v1 (internals stripped)
14:30:00 INFO    [KAFKA] produce key=SAV2001 topic=transfer.completed (ordered per key)
14:30:00 INFO    [NOTIFY] SMS: transfer of Rs.50000 to BENEF-77 for account SAV2001 (consumer never saw producer internals)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A domain event and an integration event can describe the same business fact but are completely different in scope and in the coupling they create. A domain event is internal to one bounded context — one microservice — and is handled in-process, typically through Spring Application Events with a transactional event listener so it fires after commit. Its job is to decouple side effects across aggregates inside that single service, so when a transfer completes the aggregate raises a domain event and in-process listeners recompute the daily total and refresh a fee cache rather than being called directly. Because the event never leaves the process, it can freely carry the rich internal domain model, including internal-only details, since there is no external consumer to protect.

An integration event is the opposite. It is published to a broker like Kafka precisely so other services, owned by other teams, can react, and the moment it crosses the service boundary its schema becomes a contract exactly like a public API, with every consumer coupled to it. That is why an integration event must act as an Anti-Corruption Layer, a Domain-Driven Design idea that means I deliberately translate from my internal model to a curated external representation at the boundary, exposing only the fields consumers legitimately need and never serializing my internal entity directly. If I leaked the internal model, every refactor of my internals would become a breaking change for every consumer, and I would have recreated the tight coupling microservices exist to eliminate.

I make integration events safe with three practices. I use a stable, versioned, schema-first format like Avro or Protobuf governed by a Schema Registry that enforces compatibility, so I can add fields without breaking old consumers. I key each event by the aggregate-root ID, the account ID, so all events for one account land on the same Kafka partition and are consumed in order, because out-of-order events about one account could corrupt derived balances. And I put an explicit translation step in the producer that maps the internal domain event to the external schema, which is the Anti-Corruption Layer realized in code.

At National Bank of India I wired these together with the common pattern: a domain event fires in-process when a transfer completes, internal listeners handle the internal side effects, and a translator maps that domain event into a slim, versioned integration event written to the transactional outbox in the same transaction, after which the relay publishes it to Kafka keyed by account. The notification and statement teams consumed only that versioned integration event and never saw our internal ledger references or risk buckets, so we were free to refactor our internals without ever breaking them, and per-account ordering kept their derived views correct.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is this: domain events are private, in-process, and may carry my internal model to decouple side effects inside one service, whereas integration events are public, broker-carried, versioned contracts that act as an Anti-Corruption Layer — exposing only curated fields through an Avro or Protobuf schema in a registry and keyed by the aggregate-root ID for ordering — so I never publish raw internal domain events to Kafka and thereby keep my internals free to evolve behind a stable external contract.
